sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Networks depend on logical configuration that determines how names are resolved, devices receive IP settings, networks are separated, and users connect securely from remote locations.
Objective 2.4 covers DNS records, DHCP configuration concepts, virtual LANs, and virtual private networks.
bullets: DHCP leases, reservations, scopes, and exclusions
sections.callout: DNS = find; DHCP = assign; VLAN = separate; VPN = securely connect.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes name resolution, IP assignment, logical network separation, or secure remote connectivity, can you identify the exact configuration concept?

sections.title: Domain Name System (DNS)
paragraphs: DNS lets systems locate network resources by name instead of requiring users to remember IP addresses. Different DNS records answer different questions about a name.
sections.callout: DNS records publish information about names and domains.

sections.title: A Record
paragraphs: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address.
sections.callout: Hostname needs an IPv4 address → A record.

sections.title: AAAA Record
paragraphs: An AAAA record maps a hostname to an IPv6 address.
sections.callout: Hostname needs an IPv6 address → AAAA record.

sections.title: A vs. AAAA
sections.callout: One A → IPv4; four A's → IPv6.

sections.title: Canonical Name (CNAME)
paragraphs: A Canonical Name (CNAME) record creates an alias from one hostname to another hostname. It does not directly map the alias to an IP address.
sections.callout: One hostname acts as an alias for another → CNAME.

sections.title: A Record vs. CNAME
sections.callout: A points to an address; CNAME points to a name.

sections.title: Mail Exchanger (MX)
paragraphs: An MX record identifies the mail server responsible for receiving email for a domain.
sections.callout: Which server receives email for a domain? → MX.

sections.title: Text (TXT) Record
paragraphs: A TXT record stores text information in DNS. In this objective, its important role is publishing email spam-management, authentication, and policy information for DKIM, SPF, and DMARC.
sections.callout: Publish text-based domain policy or verification information → TXT.

sections.title: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM)
paragraphs: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) uses a digital signature to help verify that a message was authorized by the sending domain and was not altered in transit. A public key is commonly published in a DNS TXT record.
sections.callout: Cryptographically signed email validation → DKIM.

sections.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
paragraphs: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) publishes which mail servers are authorized to send email for a domain. Receiving systems can compare the sending server with that policy.
sections.callout: Is this server allowed to send for the domain? → SPF.

sections.title: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
paragraphs: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM. It tells receiving systems how the domain owner wants failed or suspicious messages handled and can provide reporting.
sections.callout: Enforcement and reporting based on SPF/DKIM results → DMARC.

sections.title: DKIM vs. SPF vs. DMARC

table.caption: Email-authentication recognition
rows: Was the message signed and unchanged?
What policy applies to failed checks, and how are results reported?

sections.callout: DKIM = signature; SPF = sender; DMARC = policy.

sections.title: DNS Record Recognition
sections.callout: Address → A/AAAA; alias → CNAME; mail → MX; policy/text → TXT.

sections.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)
paragraphs: DHCP automatically provides network configuration to clients. Leases, reservations, scopes, and exclusions control how its address pool is assigned.
sections.callout: DHCP manages the address pool.

sections.title: DHCP Lease
paragraphs: A lease is the period of time a DHCP-assigned IP address is given to a client. The address is not necessarily permanent, and the client can renew the lease.
sections.callout: Borrow the IP for a defined time → lease.

sections.title: DHCP Reservation
paragraphs: A reservation ensures that a particular device receives the same address from DHCP, usually by associating the address with a device identifier such as its MAC address.
sections.callout: Use DHCP but always receive the same IP → reservation.

sections.title: DHCP Scope
paragraphs: A scope defines the range of IP addresses that a DHCP server is allowed to assign. It is the available DHCP address pool.
sections.callout: Define the range DHCP can distribute → scope.

sections.title: DHCP Exclusion
paragraphs: An exclusion removes selected addresses from the DHCP assignment range so they are not handed out dynamically.
sections.callout: Address is inside the scope but must not be assigned → exclusion.

sections.title: Lease vs. Reservation vs. Scope vs. Exclusion

table.caption: DHCP configuration concepts
rows: How long a client keeps an assignment
Which address a specific device receives
Addresses in the range DHCP must not use

sections.callout: Lease = time; reservation = device; scope = range; exclusion = block.

sections.title: DHCP Concepts Working Together
paragraphs: A scope might allow 192.168.10.100 through 192.168.10.200. An exclusion can remove .100 through .109, a reservation can save .120 for a printer, and the lease controls how long ordinary dynamic assignments last.
sections.callout: Scope opens the pool; exclusion removes part; reservation saves one; lease controls time.

sections.title: Virtual LAN (VLAN)
paragraphs: A Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) logically separates devices into different network segments even when they share physical switching infrastructure.
One managed switch can place administration, employees, and guests into separate logical networks.
sections.callout: One physical switching environment → multiple logical networks.

sections.title: Why VLANs Are Used
paragraphs: VLANs support network segmentation, organization, traffic separation, security boundaries, and reduced unnecessary broadcast traffic.
Each VLAN forms a logical broadcast domain, and routing is normally required for devices in different VLANs to communicate.
sections.callout: VLANs separate first; routing reconnects when allowed.

sections.title: VLAN Recognition
bullets: Share switching hardware while separating traffic
sections.callout: Logical separation on shared switching infrastructure → VLAN.

sections.title: Virtual Private Network (VPN)
paragraphs: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) creates a protected logical connection across another network, commonly the internet. It can connect remote users or separate sites to organizational resources.
sections.callout: Protected tunnel across an untrusted network → VPN.

sections.title: Remote-Access VPN
paragraphs: A remote-access VPN lets an individual device securely connect to another network, such as an employee laptop connecting to company resources from home.
sections.callout: One user or device → company network.

sections.title: Site-to-Site VPN
paragraphs: A site-to-site VPN connects two networks through a protected logical link across another network, such as linking two offices over the internet.
sections.callout: Network → network.

sections.title: VLAN vs. VPN

table.caption: Virtual network concepts
rows: Logically separates devices inside network infrastructure
Securely connects users or networks across another network

sections.callout: VLAN = segment; VPN = tunnel.

sections.title: Configuration Map
bullets: DNS: A → IPv4; AAAA → IPv6; CNAME → alias; MX → mail; TXT → text/policy
Email authentication: DKIM → signature; SPF → authorized sender; DMARC → policy/reporting
DHCP: lease → time; reservation → device; scope → range; exclusion → blocked addresses

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: DNS text or policy information → TXT
Same DHCP address for one device → reservation
Addresses DHCP must not distribute → exclusions
Secure remote or network connection → VPN

sections.title: Objective 2.4 Exam Trap
paragraphs: Identify the job first: DNS finds, DHCP assigns, VLAN separates, and VPN connects securely. Then choose the exact configuration concept.

entries.title: A vs. AAAA
paragraphs: Look at the IP version: A maps to IPv4; AAAA maps to IPv6.

entries.title: A vs. CNAME
paragraphs: A maps a name to an IPv4 address; CNAME maps a name to another name.

entries.title: MX vs. TXT
paragraphs: MX identifies where domain mail goes; TXT stores text such as email-authentication information.

entries.title: DKIM vs. SPF vs. DMARC
paragraphs: DKIM is signature, SPF is authorized sender, and DMARC is policy/reporting.

entries.title: Scope vs. Exclusion
paragraphs: A scope defines addresses DHCP may assign; an exclusion removes addresses DHCP must not assign.

entries.title: Reservation vs. Static IP
paragraphs: A reservation still uses DHCP to provide a consistent address. A static IP is configured directly on the device.

entries.title: Lease vs. Reservation
paragraphs: A lease controls time; a reservation controls which address a device receives.

entries.title: VLAN vs. VPN
paragraphs: A VLAN segments local infrastructure; a VPN provides a protected connection across another network.

sections.callout: DNS FIND; DHCP ASSIGN; VLAN SEPARATE; VPN CONNECT SECURELY.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Specific device gets the same DHCP IP → reservation
Logical networks on shared switching infrastructure → VLAN
Secure tunnel over another network → VPN
Remote worker to company → remote-access VPN
Office network to office network → site-to-site VPN
DNS = find; DHCP = assign; VLAN = separate; VPN = securely connect
